title: Preclinical assessment for precision medicine in myeloma
official: Optimised pre-clinical Assessment of Suitable Investigational agents for preciSion medicine in myeloma - OASIS
summary:
Background and study aims 
Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells that develops in the bone marrow. Although treatments for myeloma have improved substantially, outcomes vary considerably between patients, and the disease remains incurable for most people. At present, treatment decisions are largely based on clinical factors rather than detailed biological characteristics of an individual's cancer. Furthermore, there is limited real-world evidence describing how patients receiving standard NHS treatments perform across different molecular and genetic subgroups. 

The OASIS study (Optimised pre-clinical Assessment of Suitable Investigational agents for preciSion medicine in myeloma) is a prospective, multicentre observational study designed to collect both biological samples and real-world clinical data. 

Who can participate? 
Patients receiving standard of care treatment for multiple myeloma within the UK NHS. 

What does the study involve? 
The study will recruit approximately 400 patients and follow them for up to five years. 

Four patient cohorts will be included:
•	Newly diagnosed transplant-eligible patients receiving anti-CD38 antibody-based quadruplet induction therapy.
•	Newly diagnosed transplant-ineligible patients receiving anti-CD38 antibody-based triplet or quadruplet therapy.
•	Patients experiencing first relapse who are planned to receive belantamab mafodotin-based treatment combinations (BVd or BPd).
•	Relapsed patients planned to receive bispecific antibody therapy. 

The study collects real-world data on standard of care treatment effectiveness, including treatment response, duration of response, progression-free survival, overall survival, treatment patterns, dose modifications, adverse events and supportive care measures. This information will provide a comprehensive understanding of how current NHS myeloma treatments perform in routine clinical practice. 

In addition, blood and bone marrow samples are collected during routine clinical care to undergo detailed molecular and immune profiling. Researchers will investigate genetic alterations, immune cell characteristics and circulating tumour DNA, and will compare these findings with real-world treatment outcomes. The study also aims to develop improved laboratory models that can be used to evaluate new anti-myeloma treatments and identify biomarkers that may predict which patients are most likely to benefit from specific therapies. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
As this is a data and tissue collection study following patients receiving standard of care treatment there are no additional risks to patients and their treatment will not be affected. The results may not have implications for patients participating in the study, but by combining real-world clinical outcomes with detailed biological information, OASIS aims to improve understanding of why patients respond differently to treatment, support the development of personalised treatment approaches, optimise scheduling of existing therapies, and help identify future treatment strategies for patients with multiple myeloma.

Where is the study run from?  
The Royal Marsden Hospital, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
January 2025 to January 2034.

Who is funding the study? 
1. Royal Marsden Hospital Charitable Funds, UK.
2. NIHR Biomedical Research Centre, Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust/Institute of Cancer Research, UK.
3. GlaxoSmithKline, UK.

Who is the main contact?
rmh-tr.oasisiras209666@nhs.net

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Patients aged 18 years of age or above
2.	Patients who have consented to tissue to be used for research purposes
3.	Patients that:
3.1. Have a confirmed or suspected diagnosis of symptomatic multiple myeloma (as per revised IMWG criteria) and who
are suspected to have a >10% plasma cell population present in their bone marrow based on serologic or clinical parameters and are undergoing a bone marrow aspirate sampling for diagnostic purposes
OR 
3.2. Have relapsed and are planned to receive treatment with belantamab mafodotin in combination with either bortezomib and dexamethasone (BVd) or pomalidomide and dexamethasone (BPd), as part of routine clinical care within the NHS
OR
3.3 Have relapsed and are planned to receive bispecific antibody therapy as part of routine clinical care within the NHS
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Patients unable to give informed consent
2.	Patients with known active blood borne virus infections such as HIV, Hepatitis B or Hepatitis C, or other active blood borne infections that constitute an excess risk to handling blood or bone marrow material from the patient in the laboratory
3.	Patients participating in an interventional clinical trial involving any investigational medicinal product or medical device at the start of therapy
4.	Patients who are registered in the study on the basis of a suspected new diagnosis of myeloma but are subsequently found either to not have myeloma, or to have a related plasma cell disorder or MGUS
